items.title: The name
items.text: Coca-Cola’s registration for the OK soft drink mark issued in March 1997 and was canceled in December 2003 because no declaration of continued use was filed. The older 1978 registration expired in 1999.[^11][^12] We did not search for every OK mark Coca-Cola may hold; these are the two tied to the soda.

items.title: The drink
items.text: Phased out of its test markets from September 1995.[^9] It was never sold nationally, and we found no re-release.

items.title: The cans and posters
items.text: Daniel Clowes said in 2010 that the cans were “quite valuable.”[^14] The Believer found poster art selling for hundreds of dollars on eBay in 2014.[^13]

items.title: The makers
items.text: Peter Wegner left advertising and became an artist. Todd Waterbury was executive creative director at Target by 2014.[^13] The Washington Post reported in 1994 that their agency had won the Microsoft account partly on the basis of Coca-Cola’s faith in it.[^8]

items.title: The hotline
items.text: 1-800-I-FEEL-OK was paused in early September 1994 with a promise to return on the 12th.[^8] We could not find when it was switched off.

items.title: Fruitopia
items.text: Zyman’s other 1994 launch stayed in Coca-Cola’s product list after OK left it and was phased out in the United States in 2003, by a later account.[^3][^20]

items.title: The idea
items.text: Advertising that admits it is advertising is now ordinary, as later writers on OK point out.[^18][^17] Wegner’s verdict was that people wanted the brand and did not want the drink.[^13]

blocks.title: One owner, two dead registrations
blocks.subtitle: The name was never sold. Coca-Cola held it before the soda existed and let it go after.

nodes.what: OK is registered for soft drinks, with first use in commerce given as February 1975.[^12]
Three new applications for OK. Two are abandoned in February 1995; the third, the red-boxed mark, proceeds.[^23][^11]
OK soda goes on sale in eight or nine US test cities.[^6][^8]
The 1994 application matures into a registration, eighteen months after the product ended.[^11]
The Patent and Trademark Office cancels the 1997 registration.[^11]

nodes.owner: No live registration that we found
nodes.what: Both records were dead when checked on October 8, 2026. No drink is sold under the name.[^11][^12]

blocks.source: US Patent and Trademark Office, Trademark Status and Document Retrieval[^11][^12][^23]; Time[^6]; The Washington Post[^8]; The New York Times[^9].
